clue.text: Choose a line to read out for villain

indicators.note: Reading something out means saying it, so the phrase before it is to be heard, not spelt.

blocks.note: choose = pick, and a line of seats or plants is a row

explanation.surface: An actor choosing which line to deliver when playing the villain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a stage rehearsal, so 'read out' looks like reciting a script. It is the instruction to say PICK A ROW aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A picaro is a rogue, the roguish hero of Spanish picaresque novels, so a villain of the lovable kind.

clue.text: Part taken by 12 Across is torturous for player

indicators.note: Only a part of the words that follow is taken, so the answer lies inside them.

blocks.note: 12 Across is THESPIAN, so the string reads thesPIAN IS Torturous

explanation.surface: An actor finds a stage role agony to play.
explanation.walkthrough: You need 12 Across first: once it is THESPIAN, the letters run on from its tail into 'is torturous'. This answer is the theme: many other clues say '1 Down' meaning a named pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Player is a plain synonym here: someone who plays an instrument, and the piano is the one this whole puzzle keeps returning to.

clue.text: Musical overture from concert 1 Down

indicators.note: An overture is the opening of a piece, so it asks for the opening letter of the next word.

blocks.note: first letter of concert
Dame Myra Hess, the British pianist famous for her wartime National Gallery concerts

explanation.surface: The opening number of a concert given by a pianist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective describing the overture; it is a noun, the definition. 1 Down means 'a pianist', and here that is Myra Hess.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is the 1980s stage musical by Tim Rice and the ABBA songwriters.

clue.text: As hat may be when lacking an edge, lacking an edge – lacking an edge!

indicators.note: An edge of a word is its first or last letter, so the word loses one end: here its front.

blocks.clueFragment: As hat may be when lacking an edge
blocks.note: a hat with no brim is brimless

explanation.surface: An exasperated riddle that keeps saying the same thing about a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase does three jobs: inside the hat description it means no brim, then it knocks the edge letter B off BRIMLESS, and finally it defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rim is an edge, so rimless means without an edge, as in rimless glasses.

clue.text: Reportedly, army post was combative

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the next words are to be heard.

blocks.note: a fort is a military post; said with the R dropped, as southern British speech does

explanation.surface: A news report that a garrison put up a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound match only holds in non-rhotic British English, where the R of FORT goes unsaid.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym by tense: someone who was combative took part in a fight, and the past tense of fight carries the same sense.

clue.text: Valve released in reverse?

indicators.note: The two words of the phrase swap places, back one first, while each keeps its own spelling.

blocks.note: released = let out

explanation.surface: A valve that lets things out the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In reverse' turns the words round, not the letters, which is why no letter-by-letter turnaround works.
explanation.definitionFit: A valve is a vent, an outlet that lets gas or liquid escape.

clue.text: Fly open, ably sorted out after last bit of wiggling

indicators.note: Sorting letters out puts them in a new order.
The sorted letters come after the single letter.
The last bit of a word is its final letter.

blocks.note: last letter of wigglinG
anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Someone wriggling to do up or undo their trouser fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The fly here is not a zip: it is the verb, to travel by air.
explanation.definitionFit: Fly here is the travel verb, as in 'we fly to Rome tomorrow', meaning take a flight as a passenger rather than flap wings.

clue.text: Cheers before drunk drank – pint in that?

indicators.note: The first piece goes before the next one.
A drunk word staggers, so its letters are mixed up.

blocks.note: ta is British slang for thanks, which cheers also means
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A toast, then a pint downed from something.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers in Britain can mean thanks as well as a toast, and that is how it gives TA.
explanation.definitionFit: A tankard is a large beer mug, which a pint might be served in.

clue.text: Mark on musical score held, Estonian duets played

indicators.note: Letters that are played with are moved around.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.surface: Duets from Estonia being performed from a marked-up score.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word sits in the music room, so 'played' reads as performance rather than the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A note marked on the score to be held for its full length, with a tenuto line or fermata, is a note kept sounding.

clue.text: Meet character in Jack, say

blocks.note: to face someone is to meet them
a card is a character, an eccentric joker

explanation.surface: Meeting a colourful fellow called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack looks like a man's name; it is the playing card. The answer runs on into 15 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack is a face card, one of the court cards with a picture.

clue.text: Hustler, 1 Down nabs fresh bun with tea

indicators.note: To nab is to seize, so the pianist's name grabs the other letters and holds them inside.
Fresh letters are made anew, rearranged.

blocks.note: Thelonious Monk, the jazz pianist
anagram fodder: BUN and TEA

explanation.surface: A con man at a café grabbing a fresh bun with his tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'with' joins BUN to TEA inside the anagram. The pianist is the jazz great Monk.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountebank is a swindler, originally a quack selling cures from a bench, so a hustler.

clue.text: Delicate material put out on time

indicators.note: In an across clue, one piece on another comes after it.

blocks.note: t = time
to issue is to put out, as a publisher does

explanation.surface: A fragile fabric released on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On time' reads as punctual; it is ISSUE placed after T.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: tissue is a fine, thin fabric or paper, the kind used for wrapping gifts or blowing noses.

clue.text: Player in turn penning one article after another

indicators.note: To pen is to shut in, like sheep in a pen.
The container comes after the other piece.

blocks.note: the second article: the definite article THE
a spin is a turn
the indefinite article, A

explanation.surface: A performer writing a series of articles one after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One article after another' sounds like a prolific journalist. Both A and THE are articles, which is how one clause yields two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Player in its stage sense: the word comes from Thespis, the legendary first Greek actor, and now means any actor.

clue.text: Nobody in fact?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a person of no importance, an anonymous nobody
read literally, someone inside a fact: a person reduced to a number in the figures

explanation.walkthrough: 'In fact' looks like 'actually'; read it as 'within a fact', and the nobody is a person reduced to a number in the figures.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone treated as just a statistic is an anonymous nobody among the data.

clue.text: Retuned, cornet went briefly – would that be symbolic for 1 Down?

definitions.text: would that be symbolic for 1 Down?

indicators.note: Retuning changes the notes, and here the letters.
Brief means cut short, so the word loses its last letter.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
went = left, cut short

explanation.surface: A brass player retunes and leaves quickly, and a pianist wonders about the notation.
explanation.walkthrough: The question expects the answer no: pianists read treble and bass clefs, and the tenor clef belongs to cellos, bassoons and trombones. The C of the anagram ends up leading CLEF.
explanation.definitionFit: A clef is the symbol at the start of a stave; the tenor clef is a C clef set for tenor-range instruments.

clue.text: See 9
Female relative in grandma? Untrue

indicators.note: The answer sits inside the words that follow.

blocks.note: grandmA UNTrue

explanation.surface: Doubt over whether a woman is really someone's grandmother.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark breaks the phrase in the surface but not in the letters, which run straight across it.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a relative of the parents' generation, the sister of a mother or father or the wife of an uncle.

clue.text: 1 Down secures first place in competition – to be a decent player?

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast inside.
First place in a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: Winifred Atwell, the Trinidad-born pianist who topped the British charts in the 1950s
first letter of competition

explanation.surface: A pianist winning a contest, and so showing they are a good player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First place in competition' looks like winning; it is just the letter C. Player shifts from the pianist to an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a good actor performs convincingly, and player shifts sense from the pianist to someone on stage.

clue.text: Old tennis player with effortlessness defending Act of Congress

blocks.note: Ivan Lendl, world number one in the 1980s
ease = effortlessness

explanation.surface: A retired tennis star, playing easily, holding off a bill in Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defending' looks like the verb joining the tennis player to the Act; it belongs to the definition, since the 1941 law was titled an Act to promote the defense of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Lend-Lease was the 1941 US Act supplying arms to Britain and its allies to help defend the United States.

clue.text: 1 Down inspiring good singer

indicators.note: To inspire is literally to breathe in, so the name takes the letter inside.

blocks.note: Fats Domino, the rock and roll pianist
g = good

explanation.surface: A pianist inspiring a fine vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good singer' reads as one phrase; good is the G that goes inside, and singer stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Plácido Domingo is the Spanish operatic tenor, one of the Three Tenors.

clue.text: That man overcome by mood, part of ode sung

indicators.note: In a down clue, a piece overcome by another has the other on top of it, above it.

blocks.note: a strop is a British word for a bad mood, a sulk
he = that man

explanation.surface: A man in a sulk while a stanza of an ode is sung.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the thing overcome sits underneath. Strop is British slang: to be in a strop is to be in a huff.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek drama the strophe is the first section of a choral ode, sung while the chorus moved one way.

clue.text: Mouse wee in one’s ear?

indicators.note: What is in the ear is heard, so the word is taken by sound.

blocks.note: wee is Scottish and British for small, which is mini

explanation.surface: A tiny mouse creeping into someone's ear.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee looks like the verb, and it is the adjective for tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnie Mouse is Mickey's Disney companion.

clue.text: Archer perhaps with string as tight

indicators.note: Tight is British slang for drunk, and drunk letters are jumbled.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: An archer whose bowstring is drawn taut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' belongs to the bow in the surface; as slang for drunk it means the letters are mixed. The archer is Sagittarius.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archer is Sagittarius, one of the twelve star signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: What I find tender in Indian city?

blocks.note: what belongs to I is my
somewhere you find tender is sore

explanation.surface: A visitor with a painful spot somewhere in India.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together it is 'my sore': the spot I find tender. The city, now officially Mysuru, is in Karnataka.
explanation.definitionFit: Mysore is a city in the south Indian state of Karnataka.

clue.text: Southern bloke cut short defending wife – ‘e flipped?

indicators.note: The word loses its last letter.
Defenders surround what they protect, so the letters go round W.

blocks.note: s = southern
bloke = chap, minus its last letter
w = wife

explanation.surface: A cockney-sounding story of a southern man who snapped.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H in ‘e reads as a southern accent. In fact it is the letter e, and the schwa's phonetic symbol is an e turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa, the neutral vowel sound, is written ə, an upside-down e.

clue.text: 1 Down on back of cow – something afoot?

indicators.note: In an across clue, one piece on another comes after it.
The back of a word is its last letter.

blocks.note: last letter of coW
Duke Ellington, jazz pianist and bandleader

explanation.surface: A pianist riding on a cow's back.
explanation.walkthrough: Afoot usually means happening; here it means on a foot. A wellington is a rubber boot, handy around cows.
explanation.definitionFit: A wellington, or welly, is a waterproof rubber boot, something worn on the foot.

clue.text: Native Americans shaving 1 Down

indicators.note: Shaving takes a thin layer off the outside, here the letter at each end.

blocks.note: Frédéric Chopin, the Polish composer and pianist

explanation.surface: A tribe giving a pianist a shave.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaving CHOPIN removes C and N from the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hopi are a Native American people of northeastern Arizona.

clue.text: Organ in song amplified

indicators.note: The first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: an organ is a newspaper, and FT is the Financial Times
a Lied is a German art song

explanation.surface: An organ piece within a song is turned up louder.
explanation.walkthrough: Organ looks like the instrument; it is a newspaper, the Financial Times. Lied is German for song, familiar from Schubert.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifted means raised or boosted, as a sound is when amplified.

clue.text: 1 Down fed a herb

indicators.note: Food goes inside, so the name takes A into it.

blocks.note: Victor Borge, the Danish-American comic pianist
the word itself

explanation.surface: A pianist being given some herb to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Borge was famous for mixing piano playing with comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Borage is a herb with blue star-shaped flowers, used in salads and Pimm's.
